In this review, we highlight recent methodological developments in click chemistry-based protein labeling and their applications in neurobiology.

title: Nasal In Situ Hydrogels: A Boon For Anti-Emetic Drug Delivery.
journal: Critical reviews in therapeutic drug carrier systems
abstract: Nasal route presents an alternative avenue for achieving local or systemic drug effects owing to its non-invasiveness, expansive surface area, rapid drug absorption, and circumvention of first-pass effect. It offers a promising route for brain targeting too, as it bypasses the blood-brain barrier, thus facilitating direct nose to brain drug delivery. However, traditional routes of administering anti-emetic drugs, primarily oral or parenteral, suffer from drawbacks like poor patient compliance and low drug bioavailability. The nasal route is a favorable alternative, albeit limited by the short retention time due to mucociliary clearance. This can be overcome by application of in situ gelling systems that undergo gelation within the nasal cavity in response to physiological cues, thereby prolonging drug retention and enhancing bioavailability. This facilitates dose reduction, reduced frequency and controlled drug release, thereby improving patient acceptance. Presently, various formulations utilizing intranasal in situ gelling approaches are under development for anti-emetic drugs. These formulations employ stimuli-responsive mechanisms such as thermosensitivity, ion responsiveness, and pH sensitivity for in situ gel formation, with a focus on employing specific polymers tailored to these stimuli. The article highlights importance of nasal delivery of anti-emetic drugs and studies done on this topic till date. Intranasal in situ gelling systems hold promise due to their ease of administration, prolonged nasal retention, improved patient compliance and enhanced bioavailability, positioning them as efficient alternatives to conventional routes of administration.

title: Brain-iT Immunotherapy: The Neurotransmitters Dopamine, Glutamate, GnRH-II and Neuropeptide Y Revive, Activate and Empower Healthy T Cells, Exhausted T Cells of Cancer Patients, and Genetically Engineered CAR T Cells.
abstract: Neurotransmitters are critical signaling molecules of the nervous system that activate their receptors within milliseconds, and convey accurate, coordinated, tightly regulated and important messages from one nerve cell, across a synapse, to another nerve, muscle or gland cell. It is time to realize that specific neurotransmitters also activate T cells directly and rapidly via their receptors in T cells. Subsequently, they decrease immune checkpoint inhibitors, increase expression of critical receptors, and induce a kaleidoscope of effector T cell functions. This review summarizes our discoveries of direct, activating, rejuvenating, and strengthening effects of either Dopamine, Glutamate, GnRH-II or Neuropeptide Y, or their combinations on human T cells of five origins: (1) normal T cells of healthy people, (2) exhausted T cells of head and neck cancer patients, (3) exhausted T cells of hepatocellular carcinoma patients, (4) exhausted T cells of glioblastoma patients, and (5) human genetically-engineered CAR T cells. The beneficial effects of these neurotransmitters on healthy T cells and on exhausted T cells of cancer patients include the following: depolarization; simultaneous decreased expression of key checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1, LAG-3, Tim-3, TIGIT and CD160); increased expression of CD3 zeta chain, CD147/EMM-PRIN/Basigin and 67kDa laminin receptor; and increased adhesion to fibronectin and laminin, chemotactic migration to SDF-1, migration toward autologous tumors, gene expression, cytokine secretion, proliferation, and arrest of human cancer cells. The direct effects of GnRH-II, Dopamine, or Glutamate on human anti-breast cancer ErbB-2+ CAR T cells were discovered in a yet unpublished collaborative research with Professor Zelig Eshhar, the pioneering scientist who invented and developed the concept of T-bodies, later re-named CAR T cells. The direct effects of the neurotransmitters on these CAR T cells include (1) dramatically increased expression of: CD3 zeta, CD147 and CXCR4, within only 30 minutes; (2) increased chemotactic migration towards SDF-1; (3) increased migration toward breast cancer cells; (4) increased penetration of the bone marrow of SCID mice; (5) increased homing to human breast cancer in SCID mice; and (6) increased inhibition of human breast cancer in SCID mice. In summary, either Glutamate, Dopamine, Neuropeptide Y, GnRH-II or their combinations, can activate, rescue, and strengthen healthy, exhausted, and genetically engineered CAR T cells. A novel personalized adoptive immunotherapy, called Brain-iT Immunotherapy, was invented and patented, and the review details its diagnostic and therapeutic stages for either patient's exhausted T cells or genetically engineered CAR T cells.

title: LDH-related Metabolic Alterations in Alzheimer's Disease: Evidence from Clinical and Transcriptomic Analyses.
abstract: Reduced brain energy metabolism is a key feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD); however, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)-related metabolic changes in AD are not fully understood. This study aimed to evaluate serum LDH activity in patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and AD. We used public transcriptomic datasets to explore the features of LDHA and LDHB across brain regions, cell types, and co-expression networks. In a retrospective clinical cohort of 132 healthy controls (HC), 87 patients with MCI, and 103 patients with AD, we compared serum LDH activity after adjusting for major clinical covariates. Next, we used public transcriptomic datasets [AlzData, Agora, CELLxGENE, and genotype-tissue expression (GTEx)] to evaluate regional and cell-type-specific expression patterns of LDHA and LDHB. We also characterized LDH-associated functional networks using GTEx normal brain data for baseline co-expression analysis and AD-related weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Clinical cohort analysis showed that serum LDH activity was significantly decreased in patients with MCI and AD. Serum LDH activity did not significantly correlate with mini-mental state examination (MMSE) or montreal cognitive assessment (MoCA) scores. Brain transcriptomic analysis revealed that LDHA expression was significantly downregulated in AD-related regions (entorhinal cortex, hippocampus, and temporal cortex), whereas LDHB showed a downward trend in several AD-related regions. Both genes were detectable across multiple brain cell types with relatively prominent expression in neurons. Functional analysis showed that, under normal conditions, LDHA-correlated genes were broadly involved in glycolysis, vesicle trafficking, autophagy, and proteostasis, whereas LDHB-correlated genes were highly concentrated in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and the citric acid (TCA) cycle. AD-related WGCNA showed region-dependent organization of LDHA- and LDHB-containing modules, with repeated enrichment in synaptic vesicle-related processes, mitochondrial respiration, autophagy, and proteostasis-related pathways. This study provides clinical and transcriptomic evidence of LDH-related metabolic alterations in patients with AD. Reduced serum LDH activity in MCI and AD, together with decreased LDHA/LDHB expression in AD-related brain regions and region-dependent LDH-associated co-expression networks, supports a potential link between LDH-related metabolism and mitochondrial energy metabolism, synaptic function, and proteostasis in AD. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory, and require validation through paired prospective and mechanistic studies.

title: Abolition by design: implementing the dismantling of the commercial tobacco and nicotine industry.
abstract: The commercial tobacco and nicotine industry continues to drive preventable disease and death globally. Despite progress in tobacco control, industry power, product diversification, market expansion, and policy interference have constrained the impact of incremental regulatory approaches. Downstream interventions, such as cessation supports and lung cancer screening, remain essential but respond to accumulated harms rather than preventing exposure at its source. This paper presents an implementation framework that positions abolition as a staged, governable, and legally supported public health strategy. Rather than a symbolic endpoint, abolition is conceptualized as a sequenced governance process through which industry structures can be dismantled using existing regulatory, fiscal, and enforcement mechanisms. These mechanisms are embedded within national systems and international instruments, including the World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control and international human rights instruments. Abolition is mischaracterized as consumer prohibition. This reflects a category error that evaluates abolition using prohibition logics, obscuring its focus on dismantling corporate production, supply, and profit infrastructures through existing governance and regulatory tools. The framework conceptualizes the industry as an ecosystem spanning corporate structures, product categories, supply chains, science distortion, and political influence. Each domain is mapped to disruption levers and institutions, with the aim of reducing implementation risk and limiting industry adaptation. Abolition is framed as a coordinated governance project across local, national, and global levels, with Indigenous peoples and young people recognized as leaders shaping accountability, prevention pathways, and norms. This approach illustrates how abolition-oriented reform may be administratively feasible, legally defensible, and relevant to advancing health equity.

title: Embryonic Depletion of D-Aspartate Perturbs NMDA Receptor-Dependent Long-Term Potentiation in the Hippocampus of Juvenile Mice.
abstract: D-Aspartate (D-Asp) is an endogenous NMDA receptor agonist that exhibits a pronounced developmental peak in the mammalian brain, suggesting a regulatory role in glutamatergic signaling and neurodevelopment. Disruption of D-Asp homeostasis has been associated with neuropsychiatric disorders characterized by early-life circuit vulnerability, including schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders. However, its impact on hippocampal physiology remains incompletely defined. Here, we investigated how constitutive D-Asp depletion affects synaptic function in the hippocampal CA1 region of Ddo-knock-in (Ddo-KI) mice, in which zygotic overexpression of the D-Asp-degrading enzyme, D-aspartate oxidase (DDO or DASPO), results in embryonic and persistent D-Asp deficiency. Electrophysiological recordings were performed in acute hippocampal slices from male and female mice at postnatal Day 30 (P30) and Day 60 (P60). Analysis of basal synaptic transmission, assessed through paired-pulse ratio and spontaneous excitatory/inhibitory events, revealed no significant genotype-dependent differences. In contrast, NMDA receptor (NMDAR)-dependent synaptic plasticity was selectively altered, as theta-burst stimulation induced significantly greater long-term potentiation (LTP) in juvenile P30 Ddo-KI mice. This paradoxical enhancement was no longer observed at P60, indicating that the phenotype is developmentally restricted. Patch-clamp recordings further revealed a reduced AMPAR/NMDAR ratio in P30 Ddo-KI males, suggesting an altered balance between AMPAR- and NMDAR-mediated synaptic currents. Importantly, acute bath application of exogenous D-Asp rapidly restored LTP to wild-type levels, indicating that the electrophysiological phenotype is acutely reversible and sensitive to D-Asp availability. Biochemical analyzes confirmed increased DASPO activity and reduced D-Asp levels in Ddo-KI mice at both ages examined, indicating that the age-dependent plasticity phenotype is unlikely to result from age-dependent changes in D-Asp catabolism. Overall, these findings demonstrate that early developmental D-Asp deficiency induces a paradoxical, juvenile-specific enhancement of hippocampal NMDAR-dependent synaptic plasticity, highlighting the importance of D-Asp homeostasis during brain development.

title: Modernizing Canada's Regulations for Clinical Trials in Medical Emergencies.
journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques

title: Landscape of Canadian Stroke Motor and Cognitive Rehabilitation Trials: Trends, Strengths and Future Directions.
journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques
abstract: This study aims to systematically identify and describe all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating post-stroke motor and cognitive rehabilitation conducted in Canada, within the broader context of global post-stroke rehabilitation research. The present secondary descriptive/bibliometric analysis used data derived from five integrated systematic reviews conducted by the same research group, from inception to 2024. A subset of data was examined in Canadian trials, including number of RCTs, sample size, participant sex, time post-stroke, methodological quality, intervention types and outcome measures. In total, 106 out of 3602 global RCTs were conducted in Canada. Canadian RCT relative contribution to global research has slowed down over time. Sample size was significantly smaller in the chronic post-stroke phase compared to acute and subacute phases in both Canadian (p = 0.013) and global trials (p < 0.001). Compared to global trials, Canadian RCTs had comparable sample size (p = 0.72) and methodological quality (p = 0.94) but were more likely to be conducted in the chronic phase (p = 0.001), evaluate exercise-based and rehabilitation-oriented interventions and assess activity and participation outcome measures. Chronic trials were more likely to be led by academic therapists (p = 0.031), while the acute and subacute trials were more likely to be led by academic physicians (p = 0.003). Canadian RCTs have made important contributions to stroke rehabilitation research. However, expanding research into earlier recovery phases, integrating technology-driven interventions and incorporating outcome measures across all three International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health domains will be important to strengthening Canada's impact and advancing stroke rehabilitation evidence.

title: Expanded EP-QuIC Testing for Sporadic CJD in a Local Geographic Area of Canada Results in Improved Surveillance.
journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques
abstract: Diagnosis of sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) has traditionally relied on non-specific cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers such as 14-3-3γ and total tau. The development of quaking-induced conversion (QuIC) assays has enabled direct detection of prion seeds, improving antemortem diagnostic accuracy. We previously noted a high CSF submission rate from the Canadian province of New Brunswick. We leveraged this observation to evaluate how expanded regional testing influences prion disease surveillance and the diagnostic performance of EP-QuIC. CSF submissions between 2016 and 2024 from all provinces to the Public Health Agency of Canada's National Microbiology Laboratory were considered, and EP-QuIC results were analyzed in the context of biomarker profiles and patient demographics. Biochemical subtype distribution was examined to assess whether increased testing density facilitates the detection of subtypes with less common clinical presentations. The CSF submissions provided an opportunity to assess EP-QuIC performance in a cohort with increased testing rates. EP-QuIC maintained high diagnostic reliability, demonstrating strong performance even when clinical suspicion was expected to be low. Additionally, a modest rise in VV2 cases was observed, suggesting that broader testing could improve the identification of those sCJD subtypes that may not initially meet criteria for classic CJD and could otherwise be underrecognized. Enhanced regional EP-QuIC testing supports more robust prion disease surveillance and retains high diagnostic accuracy across varied clinical contexts. Increased testing density may also improve detection of some sCJD subtypes, highlighting the value of increased access to EP-QuIC testing.

title: Use of Telestroke Prior to Endovascular Stroke Treatment in Canada: Results from the OPTIMISE Registry.
journal: The Canadian journal of neurological sciences. Le journal canadien des sciences neurologiques
abstract: Telestroke allows rapid assessment of acute stroke patients for intravenous thrombolysis and endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). While its safety and efficacy for thrombolysis are well established, evidence regarding EVT decision-making via telestroke is scarce. We analysed data from Optimising Patient Treatment In Major Ischaemic Stroke with EVT (OPTIMISE), an EVT registry of Canadian comprehensive stroke centres. We compared unadjusted time metrics and procedural outcomes between patients treated with EVT evaluated via telestroke and those evaluated without telestroke. A primary analysis included all EVT cases, and a sub-analysis focused on patients transferred from another centre. Mixed-effects logistic regression, adjusted for relevant clinical and radiological confounders, was used to assess symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage (sICH), good functional outcome and all-cause mortality. Between 2018 and 2021, a total of 6803 patients received EVT across 20 centres. Patients receiving telestroke consultation had longer onset-to-EVT centre door time and onset-to-groin puncture time. In unadjusted analyses, telestroke patients had higher sICH proportions (6.5% vs. 3.1%), lower proportions of good functional outcomes (35.6% vs. 40.6%) and higher all-cause mortality (39.9% vs. 27.5%) compared to those not receiving telestroke consultation. These differences did not persist in adjusted analyses. The sub-analysis with multivariate adjustment restricted to transferred patients also revealed no differences in outcomes between the two groups. Patients evaluated with telestroke prior to EVT had longer treatment times than those not evaluated with telestroke. The higher risk for unfavourable outcomes did not persist after adjustment for confounders. There remains a strong need to optimise the delivery of EVT for patients evaluated at telestroke centres.

title: Lipid Transporter TMEM24/C2CD2L Plays Essential Roles in Retinal Photoreceptor Survival by Regulating Calcium Signaling and Synaptic Transmission.
journal: FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology
abstract: Retinal neurotransmission is fundamental to vision, relying on the precise calcium-dependent release of glutamate at photoreceptor ribbon synapses. Disruptions in this pathway underlie multiple visual disorders in humans. TMEM24/C2CD2L, an SMP domain-containing phospholipid transporter enriched at endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-plasma membrane (PM) contact sites, regulates phosphoinositide homeostasis and calcium signaling. However, its role in the retina remains unknown. Here, we show that C2CD2L is predominantly expressed in retinal photoreceptors. Using a rod-specific conditional knockout mouse, we demonstrate that loss of C2CD2L impairs rod-mediated visual function, causes progressive outer retinal degeneration, induces reactive Müller glia activation, and triggers apoptotic photoreceptor death. Transcriptomic profiling of pre-degenerative retinas revealed significant downregulation of genes associated with voltage-gated calcium channel complexes, postsynaptic density membranes, and visual perception. These changes were accompanied by severe synaptic defects, including fewer RIBEYE- and Bassoon-positive puncta, reduced ribbon-bearing terminals, shortened synaptic ribbons, and decreased ribbon-tethered synaptic vesicles. Our findings establish C2CD2L as a critical regulator of rod photoreceptor synaptic integrity, calcium-channel-associated signaling, and retinal homeostasis.

title: Altered connectivity and network efficiency in preterm infants.
abstract: Preterm birth is associated with altered maturation of large-scale functional brain networks during the neonatal period. Acquisition and preprocessing variability across neonatal resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) studies limits cross-site comparability and may obscure prematurity-related alterations. We combined rs-fMRI data from 90 local preterm infants scanned at term-equivalent age (TEA) with data from 160 infants in the Developing Human Connectome Project (100 term-born and 60 preterm) to evaluate cross-site harmonization and characterize edge-wise functional connectivity and network efficiency. Data were preprocessed using an identical pipeline in SPM and CONN toolbox, harmonized with neuroCombat, and analyzed using per-edge analysis of covariance for connectivity and linear mixed-effects models for graph efficiency. Harmonization substantially reduced site-related variance and improved cross-site comparability. Relative to term-born controls, preterm infants showed widespread edge-wise hypoconnectivity, with only limited focal hyperconnectivity. Graph-theoretical analysis revealed reduced local alongside modestly increased global network efficiency in preterm infants, whereas regional connection-class composition did not interact with group. These findings support the feasibility of harmonizing multi-site neonatal rs-fMRI data and suggest that prematurity at TEA is characterized by widespread functional hypoconnectivity and a shift in the balance between local network segregation and large-scale functional integration.

title: Inhibition of Cerebellar Dentate Nucleus-Zona Incerta Glutamatergic Circuit Improves Sleep Disturbances in Chronic Temporal Lobe Epilepsy Model.
abstract: Patients with chronic temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) frequently experience various sleep disorders, characterized by reduced sleep duration, diminished sleep stages, and disrupted sleep patterns. Recent research has identified a population of GABAergic neurons in the ventral zona incerta (ZI) that is instrumental in promoting sleep, along with a neural pathway that connects the cerebellar dentate nucleus (CDN) to the ZI. However, the precise role of this circuit in regulating sleep patterns remains inadequately understood. This study employed anatomical, chemogenetic, optogenetic, and immunofluorescence staining techniques to investigate the potential of the CDN-ZI circuit in ameliorating sleep disturbances associated with TLE. Our findings indicate that pilocarpine-treated mice exhibit significant sleep fragmentation and reduced sleep duration, particularly during non-rapid eye movement sleep. By employing optogenetic and chemogenetic methods to target CDN glutamatergic neurons, we observed a decrease in sleep fragmentation, an increase in overall sleep duration, and an enhancement in sleep quality in pilocarpine-treated mice. The inhibition of the CDN-ZI glutamatergic circuit through optogenetic and chemogenetic methods resulted in substantial improvements in sleep disturbances following TLE. Targeting the CDN-ZI glutamatergic circuit represents a promising therapeutic strategy for addressing sleep disorders resulting from chronic TLE.

title: Increased risk of stroke after a new cancer diagnosis-Where are the knowledge gaps currently?
Retinal Nerve Fibre Layer and Ganglion Cell Complex Thickness in Diabetes Mellitus without Diabetic Retinopathy.
journal: Nepalese journal of ophthalmology : a biannual peer-reviewed academic journal of the Nepal Ophthalmic Society : NEPJOPH
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy is on the rise and understanding mechanisms of retinal neurodegeneration in diabetes mellitus will help in halting retinopathy. The study was done to assess the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex thickness in type two diabetes mellitus without clinically evident vascular retinopathy and compare them with the normal population to understand the early neurodegenerative changes. This was a hospital-based, prospective, observational study conducted in South India from 2022 May to 2023 March. This study included one hundred and seventeen eyes with type two diabetes mellitus without clinical diabetic retinopathy and 115 normal age-matched controls after ethical approval using a consecutive sampling technique. Participants with other systemic co-morbidities and retinal pathology were excluded. Average, superior, and inferior retinal nerve fibre layer thickness and average, superior, inferior, inferonasal, superonasal, superotemporal, and inferotemporal macular ganglion cell complex thickness were measured using spectral-domain optical coherence tomography. A student's unpaired t-test was used for comparing the thickness between cases and controls, and analysed using SPSS Statistics version 26. The retinal nerve fibre layer thickness was significantly reduced in all quadrants in type two diabetes mellitus without diabetic retinopathy when compared to normal controls (p <0.001), with the mean nerve fibre layer thickness of 100.3μm ± 12.5μm in cases and 110.9μm ± 8.7μm in controls. The mean macular ganglion cell complex thickness was also significantly decreased in diabetes without retinopathy (p <0.001), with values of 99.9μm ± 8.1μm in diabetics and 109.3μm ± 4.9μm in controls. In diabetics, increased glycosylated haemoglobin correlated negatively with the nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex thickness. Neurodegeneration of the retinal nerve fibre layer and ganglion cell complex in diabetics occurs before clinically visible vascular changes appear. Higher glycosylated haemoglobin is a risk factor for early neurodegeneration.

title: Spinal microglia mediate chronic itch by promoting ferroptosis.
abstract: Chronic itch, affecting 8-10% of the global population, is a debilitating condition linked to dermatoses, systemic diseases, and neurological disorders, with limited therapeutic efficacy due to unclear central mechanisms. Spinal microglia, central nervous system-resident immune cells, regulate neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity in chronic pain and neurodegeneration, but their role in chronic itch remains unknown. This study investigated the role of spinal microglia in chronic itch. Using an allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) mouse chronic itch model, we found robust microglial activation, accompanied by c-Fos-positive neuronal activation, in the spinal dorsal horn of a chronic itch model. Pharmacological inhibition (minocycline) or genetic ablation of microglia significantly reduced mechanical itch hypersensitivity and spontaneous scratching, alongside decreased microglial/neuronal activation. Morphological and molecular analyses revealed downregulated antioxidants (glutathione peroxidase 4 [GPX4], superoxide dismutase [SOD], glutathione [GSH],) and upregulated lipid peroxidation (malondialdehyde [MDA], acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 [ACSL4]) in the spinal cord, indicating ferroptosis. Intrathecal liproxstatin-1 (ferroptosis inhibitor) alleviated itch behaviors and restored GPX4, SOD, GSH and MDA level, without affecting microglial activation. Our findings demonstrate that spinal microglia promote chronic itch by triggering ferroptosis in spinal dorsal horn. These findings provide the first evidence of microglia-ferroptosis crosstalk in chronic itch, providing a mechanistic basis for targeting glial activity or ferroptosis to develop novel therapies.

title: Isolation and Characterization of Levilactobacillus brevis FBL-3 from Godeulppaegi Kimchi and Screening of Medium Components for γ-Aminobutyric Acid Production.
abstract: γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is an amino acid with a variety of biological functions and is now becoming an essential food ingredient. In this work, a GABA-producing lactic acid bacterium was isolated from godeulppaegi kimchi and characterized by phenotypic, biochemical and molecular parameters. The isolate was identified as FBL-3, which produced acid colonies in MRS agar containing CaCO3 and L-glutamic acid, was Gram positive, catalase-negative and rod-shaped, and had 99.1% similarity to Levilactobacillus brevis by API 50 CHL analysis and 100% 16S rRNA gene sequence similarity to Lvb. brevis ATCC 14869. Further, sequence analysis of 16S rRNA gene confirmed that it was Lvb. brevis FBL-3. The effects of carbon source, nitrogen source, and L-glutamic acid concentration on cell growth and TLC-densitometrically estimated GABA production were evaluated sequentially using a one-factor-at-a-time approach. Of the carbon sources tested, xylose had the highest GABA production (12.2 ± 2.34 g/L) and dry cell weight (0.75 ± 0.00 g/L) and 10 g/L xylose was selected as a good concentration for GABA production. Yeast extract was the most promising for nitrogen sources producing 4.65 ± 0.45 g/L GABA, and 20 g/L yeast extract was selected as a practical concentration since it produced 9.12 ± 1.48 g/L GABA with lower nitrogen input than 50 g/L yeast extract. L-Glutamic acid was a necessary precursor to GABA production. Although the highest GABA titer in the L-glutamic acid concentration experiment was found for 50 g/L L-glutamic acid (19.6 ± 1.03 g/L), 10 g/L L-glutamic acid supported the highest cell growth and was considered as a more balanced precursor.

title: Long-term effects of spinal cord stimulation combined with a physiotherapist-led exercise programme and physical activity on prescription for chronic neuropathic pain.
abstract: Assess the effects of spinal cord stimulation and add-on physical activity interventions on pain, physical activity levels, and health-related quality of life. Prospective single-arm. 35 adults who underwent spinal cord stimulation device implantation for neuropathic pain completed the study. Three months after implantation, participants initiated a 6-month individualized physiotherapist-led exercise programme, followed by 12 months of physical activity on prescription. Neuropathic pain intensity (Numeric Rating Scale, 0-10), physical activity (accelerometer), and health-related quality of life (EuroQol 5-dimensions, visual analogue scale, EQ-5D VAS; 0-100) were assessed at baseline and 3, 9, and 21 months after implantation. Neuropathic pain was reduced from baseline at 9 and 21 months (mean [SD] = 6.6 [1.7] at baseline; 4.8 [2.3] at 9 months, p = 0.003; 4.8 [2.1] at 21 months, p = 0.003). EQ-5D VAS scores increased significantly by 16 (p = 0.027) and 15 (p = 0.003) points at 9 and 21 months, respectively. No changes in physical activity were observed. Changes from 3 months were not statistically significant at 9 or 21 months for any outcomes. The initial effects of spinal cord stimulation on pain and health-related quality of life remained after the introduction of physical activity interventions, with no additional improvements observed beyond 3 months after implantation.

title: Pre-driven and post-gated memristive Hopfield network: Dynamics, FPGA realization and image encryption.
journal: Neural networks : the official journal of the International Neural Network Society
abstract: Many existing memristive synaptic models merge presynaptic and postsynaptic activities into a single aggregated stimulus, making their distinct functional roles difficult to interpret. To address this issue, this paper proposes a memristive synapse with a pre-driven and post-gated state-update mechanism, in which presynaptic activity drives synaptic-state evolution while postsynaptic activity nonlinearly modulates the direction and strength of the update. The proposed synapse is embedded into a compact two-neuron memristive Hopfield neural network to investigate how this functional decomposition influences network dynamics. Equilibrium and stability analysis, bifurcation diagrams, Lyapunov exponents, and multistability analysis reveal variable-wing chaotic attractors, parameter-dependent transitions, and coexisting dynamical states. FPGA implementation verifies the hardware realizability of the proposed system, while a color-image encryption scheme demonstrates the application potential of the generated chaotic sequences. These results show that the proposed framework provides a functionally interpretable modeling route for incorporating differentiated pre/post synaptic regulation into memristive Hopfield dynamics.

title: Beyond Single-Target Therapy: Dual-Acting Cannabinoid Type-2 Receptor Modulation in Neurological Disorders.
abstract: Neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and neuroinflammatory conditions involve complex, interconnected mechanisms, including neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, cholinergic dysfunction, and synaptic impairment. The cannabinoid type-2 receptor (CB2R), primarily expressed in immune and glial cells, has emerged as a promising therapeutic target due to its role in modulating neuroinflammation and providing neuroprotection without the psychoactive effects associated with CB1R activation. Recent research highlights the potential of dual-acting CB2R ligands that also modulate CB1R, acetylcholinesterase (AChE), and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), offering a multitarget approach to neurological disorders. Although CB1R expression was identified in 1993, significant progress in designing receptor modulators began in the 2000s, with recent focus expanding to autoimmune, metabolic, and cancer-related applications. This review summarizes advances in the design, synthesis, and structure-activity relationships of CB2R-targeting ligands, emphasizing dual- or multitarget agents with cholinesterase inhibitory activity. Key chemical scaffolds include synthetic cannabinoids, heterocyclic compounds, and hybrid molecules integrating cholinesterase pharmacophores. Molecular docking and in silico studies are discussed to elucidate ligand-receptor interactions, binding modes, and determinants of selectivity. Overall, CB2R-centric dual-acting ligands represent a promising strategy for addressing multifactorial neurological disorders.

title: Treadmill Exercise Can Modulate the Inflammatory Microenvironment and Promote Regeneration After Compressive Spinal Cord Injury in Female Mice.
authors: Cavalcante Anne Caroline Rodrigues Dos Santos
journal: Journal of cellular and molecular medicine
abstract: Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) leads to severe sensorimotor impairments and reduced quality of life. Physical rehabilitation has emerged as a key therapeutic strategy to improve function and mitigate complications such as muscle atrophy and joint contractures, partly through modulation of the inflammatory microenvironment. This study investigated the effects of a structured exercise protocol on inflammation, neuroplasticity and sensorimotor recovery following compressive SCI in mice. Female C57BL/6 mice (8-12 weeks) were subjected to extradural spinal cord compression and divided into three groups: SHAM (laminectomy only), SCI (injury without treatment) and TMT (injury plus treadmill training). The TMT protocol began 7 days post-injury and continued until 56 days, with sessions performed three times per week. Functional assessments were conducted weekly, followed by electroneuromyography at 56 days and biochemical and morphological analyses after euthanasia. The TMT group demonstrated significantly improved locomotor performance and nociceptive response compared to the SCI group. Electroneuromyography revealed higher compound muscle action potential amplitudes in TMT and SHAM groups (p < 0.001). Additionally, TMT reduced muscle atrophy (p < 0.05) and increased neuromuscular junction density. Bladder wall thickness in TMT animals resembled SHAM and differed from SCI (p < 0.001), suggesting reduced inflammation. At the molecular level, TMT increased anti-inflammatory cytokines and reduced pro-inflammatory markers, alongside enhanced M2 microglial polarisation, decreased astrocyte reactivity and reduced apoptosis. Imaging analyses confirmed reduced lesion spread and fibrosis. These findings indicate that phase-adjusted exercise promotes functional recovery, neuromuscular plasticity and tissue preservation after SCI.

title: Evaluating the Effect of Positive Childhood Experiences on the Risk of Psychiatric Disorders in Early Adulthood.
abstract: While the negative impacts of traumatic childhood experiences are well established, less is known about whether positive childhood experiences (PCEs) contribute to long-term mental health. The aim of this study was to estimate the effect of PCEs on the risk of psychiatric disorders in early adulthood. Participants included 3,499 children from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children. Eligible participants were nonrandomly exposed to PCEs (e.g., "school enjoyment" or "feeling safe in neighborhood") between ages 0 and 17, measured as a score ranging from 0 to 10. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) was used to account for the likelihood of PCE exposure conditional on confounders. The effect of PCE score on risk of psychiatric disorders at age 24, using IPW- and confounder-adjusted estimates, is reported. Subgroup analysis of individual disorders was subsequently conducted. In unweighted analyses, each one-unit increase in the PCE score was associated with a 12% decrease in the odds of psychiatric disorder (odds ratio=0.88, 95% CI=0.82, 0.95). In the IPW- and confounder-adjusted model, this effect was retained (odds ratio=0.89, 95% CI=0.82, 0.95). Robust associations between PCEs and lower odds of depressive disorder (odds ratio=0.84, 95% CI=0.76, 0.93) and generalized anxiety disorder (odds ratio=0.91, 95% CI=0.84, 0.99) were found. The findings for PCE score and psychotic disorder were inconclusive. The findings indicate that PCEs are associated with reduced odds of meeting criteria for psychiatric disorders in early adulthood, particularly depression. Further research should explore PCEs as a potential preventive strategy that might reduce the burden of psychiatric disorders in early adulthood.

title: Integrated physical, cognitive and psychological rehabilitation following multiple ACL reconstructions in a professional handball player: a case report.
abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries with repeated surgical interventions and postoperative complications pose a major challenge in sports rehabilitation. Beyond neuromuscular deficits, psychological and cognitive readiness often remain impaired, increasing reinjury risk and threatening athletic careers. This case highlights an integrated rehabilitation strategy addressing physical, psychological, and cognitive domains in a professional athlete with a complex surgical history. A 31-year-old white Serbian male professional handball player with a history of two ACL reconstructions, meniscal repairs, a postoperative knee infection, and multiple arthroscopic interventions presented with persistent knee instability, pain, and psychological distress. Following repeated failed return-to-play attempts, he underwent a ten-week intervention combining therapeutic exercises, sports psychology sessions, and neurocognitive dual-task training. Pre- and post-intervention assessments included gait analysis, postural control, strength testing, ACL-specific functional tests, and psychological evaluations. Post-intervention assessments showed improvements in gait mechanics, postural stability, neuromuscular strength, and reduced functional asymmetries, alongside lower cognitive anxiety and greater motivation. This case suggests that an interdisciplinary, multimodal rehabilitation approach, integrating physical, psychological, and cognitive strategies, may help address both physical deficits and psychological barriers in athletes with multiple ACL surgeries and complex postoperative courses. Such integration may support function, confidence, and readiness in high-performance athletes facing career-threatening injuries.

title: U2 snRNP inhibition hampers pancreatic cancer cell viability by disrupting DNA repair proficiency and mitotic checkpoint integrity.
journal: Journal of experimental & clinical cancer research : CR
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer with remarkably poor prognosis. Splicing dysregulation is emerging as a hallmark and possible therapeutic target of PDAC. We performed high-throughput RNA sequencing analyses in PANC-1 cells treated with three drugs targeting the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (U2 snRNP): Pladienolide B, Thailanstatin A and Indisulam. The efficacy of splicing inhibitors, Talazoparib, Alisertib, AZD7762 and Barisertib, alone or in combination, was assessed in PDAC cells and patient-derived organoids (PDOs) by cell viability assays. RT-PCR, western blot and cell cycle assays were performed to evaluate the expression of DNA repair and mitotic genes and the execution of mitosis. PANC-1 cells were engineered to stably co-express GFP-tagged H2b histone and RFP-tagged β-tubulin by CRISPR/Cas-9 technology and used for time-lapse confocal microscopy and immunofluorescence analyses. Genes encoding for the U2 snRNP, which recognizes the 3' splice site, are upregulated in advanced PDAC. U2 snRNP-targeting drugs impair the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway in homologous recombination-proficient PDAC cells and PDOs, thus enhancing their sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. Genes whose splicing was disrupted by all three drugs are characterized by higher expression, more exon-intron junctions, weak 5' splice sites and atypical GC content. These features are enriched in mitotic genes (e.g. AURKA, AURKB, CHEK1), whose expression is strongly deregulated by splicing perturbation. Accordingly, splicing inhibition causes severe mitotic defects, leading to the accumulation of cells with misaligned condensed chromosomes on monopolar or bipolar spindles. Notably, high expression of AURKA, AURKB and CHEK1 correlates with poor prognosis in PDAC patients, whereas combined treatments with inhibitors of these mitotic kinases strongly impair the viability of PDAC cells and PDOs. These findings uncover gene features associated with sensitivity to splicing inhibitors in PDAC cells and suggest that the DDR and mitosis are biological processes highly sensitive to splicing perturbation.

title: Correction: A brain-penetrant chimeric protein combines direct glioma targeting with myeloid cell-mediated immune reprogramming.
Physical pain and risk of suicide and non-fatal self-harm among Swedish construction workers followed over three decades.
journal: Journal of occupational medicine and toxicology (London, England)
abstract: This observational cohort study aimed to investigate the extent to which physical pain increases the long-term risk of suicidal behavior among construction workers. In 1989-93, 79,099 men from the Swedish construction workers cohort completed a questionnaire on working conditions and physical symptoms, including pain, in addition to their routine health examination. The participants assessed how often they had experienced pain in nine anatomical areas over the past year; this was summarized into four categories describing pain in the neck, shoulders and upper back; the lower back and hip; the upper limbs (hand, wrist, elbow); and the lower limbs (foot, ankle, knee). Frequent pain in at least one location, as well as location-specific frequencies, were considered main exposures. Multivariable Cox proportional hazard regression was used to examine associations between pain and risk of (1) suicide, and (2) non-fatal self-harm including suicide attempt, censored at emigration, disability pension, retirement, other causes of death and end of follow-up in 2018. 55% of workers reported frequent pain in at least one location, with lower back being the most common site. Frequent pain increased the risk of non-fatal self-harm by 25% compared to no pain in any location and the risk of suicide was doubled. Frequent pain in hand, wrist or elbow was associated with excess risk of both fatal and non-fatal self-harm, while frequent pain in foot, ankle or knee was associated with non-fatal self-harm only, independent of socio-demographic factors, parental origin, body mass index, height and blood pressure. After adjustment for occupational group and unfavorable working position, the increased risk associated with pain in the limbs remained. Our findings underscore the importance of recognizing and addressing the psychological consequences of physical pain among construction workers, particularly when the pain affects the arms or legs.

title: Feeling safe: an empirical-ethical analysis of vulnerability in (es)ketamine treatment.
abstract: Treatments with acute consciousness-altering effects, such as (es)ketamine, place patients in a state of heightened vulnerability with reduced capacity for self-advocacy and self-regulation. Since feeling safe is a precondition for consenting to begin, and remaining in, treatment, this raises distinct ethical demands on care. Which features of the setting enable patients to feel safe, and how patients' and clinicians' understandings of the treatment relate to these requirements, remains unclear. This study identifies patient-, clinician- and setting-related factors shaping the experience of safety during (es)ketamine treatment and derives ethically grounded recommendations, distinguishing clinical safety, felt safety and ethical protection and analyzing their relations through a framework of induced, layered vulnerability. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 14 patients who had received intranasal esketamine (Spravato®) or IV ketamine infusion treatment and 10 clinicians administering these treatments in German psychiatric settings, and analyzed using structuring qualitative content analysis complemented by type-building analysis. Pre-treatment concerns and the experience of safety were analyzed from the patient interviews; clinician interviews informed the broad coding and the comparison of patients' and clinicians' models of ketamine's mechanism of action. Three types of pre-treatment concern, three overlapping modes of experiencing safety, and three models of ketamine's mechanism of action were identified, each associated with distinct treatment requirements. Therapeutic presence, active physical grounding, and structured post-acute transitional support ("landing aid") were described by participants as central to feeling safe. Clinicians more often conceived of ketamine as a catalyst of transformation, patients as temporary relief or symptom management, indicating potential misalignment regarding preparation and integration. Safety in (es)ketamine treatment is relationally created and individually differentiated rather than uniform, supporting an ethical case for flexible, patient-centered care above a non-negotiable floor of clinical safety. Because patients in altered states depend acutely on those who induced that state, minor clinician behaviors and the post-acute transition carry moral weight bearing on informed consent and the duty of care, yet are modifiable with few resources. Recommendations are graded by strength; one is restricted against our own empirical finding where the vulnerability analysis requires it. As an exploratory study, the findings require confirmation in larger, more diverse samples.

title: Longitudinal changes in PCOS-related reproductive and metabolic markers in female patients with bipolar disorder: a six-month observational study.
abstract: Female patients with bipolar disorder (BD) have a relatively high burden of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)-related reproductive abnormalities. This six-month longitudinal observational study aimed to examine changes in PCOS incidence and PCOS-related reproductive and metabolic markers in drug-naive female patients with BD managed without medication, with valproate (VPA), or with non-VPA mood stabilizers. A total of 72 drug-naive female outpatients with BD were recruited, and 50 patients ultimately completed the six-month follow-up. At the baseline and six-month time points, the menstrual status of each subject was recorded, the levels of sex hormones and routine metabolic indicators were measured, and ovarian ultrasound examinations were performed. The diagnosis of PCOS was carried out according to the Rotterdam criteria. After six months, no statistically significant increase in PCOS incidence was observed in any treatment group. In the No-Drug group, PCOS incidence and related reproductive indicators did not significantly worsen. In the VPA group, PCOS incidence showed a nonsignificant numerical increase, while oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), and free androgen index (FAI) increased significantly after follow-up. These findings suggest longitudinal changes in PCOS-related reproductive markers. In this exploratory six-month longitudinal observational study, early-stage female BD patients with relatively mild symptoms did not show a statistically significant increase in PCOS incidence when untreated. VPA treatment was associated with significant increases in oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, AMH, and FAI, suggesting changes in PCOS-related reproductive markers. These findings support careful reproductive and metabolic monitoring when VPA is prescribed to women with BD, while larger and longer-term studies are needed to clarify the long-term clinical trajectory of these reproductive marker changes.

title: Ocular surface outcomes after upper-eyelid-sparing management of large lower-eyelid tumor defects.
abstract: To evaluate long-term ocular surface outcomes after upper-eyelid-sparing management of large lower-eyelid defects. Twelve patients with large lower-eyelid defects after tumor excision were managed without surgical involvement of the upper eyelid using either laissez-faire (secondary intention, n = 11) healing or primary closure under tension (n = 1). The operated eye was compared with the contralateral, non-operated eye. Assessments included the Dry Eye Questionnaire-5 (DEQ-5), margin- reflex distance (MRD) 1 and 2, tear break-up time (TBUT), tear meniscus height (TMH), ocular staining score (OSS), and infrared meibography. No significant differences in TBUT or TMH were observed between operated and contralateral eyes, suggesting preserved tear film stability and tear volume despite lower-eyelid gland loss. Lower-eyelid meibography demonstrated a significant reduction in meibomian gland area in operated eyes, reflecting gland excision during tumor removal. Operated eyes showed significantly higher MRD2, DEQ-5 scores and OSSs, indicating greater exposure, subjective dry-eye symptoms, and ocular surface involvement. Upper-eyelid-sparing management of large lower-eyelid defects preserves tear film stability on long-term follow-up but is associated with increased dry-eye symptoms and ocular surface staining. Thus, preservation of the upper eyelid and its meibomian glands appears sufficient to maintain functional tear film integrity despite substantial lower-eyelid gland loss, providing guidance for surgical decision-making to minimize postoperative ocular surface morbidity.

title: Platelet P2Y12 inhibitor use and risk of colorectal cancer incidence and colorectal cancer-related mortality: a Swedish registry-based cohort study.
abstract: Low-dose aspirin use is associated with reduced CRC incidence and CRC-related mortality. A similar association with P2Y12 inhibitor use remains uncertain. We investigated whether the use of P2Y12 inhibitors was associated with CRC incidence and CRC-related mortality among individuals diagnosed with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). From the ESPRESSO cohort, we identified 334,882 patients diagnosed with ASCVD between 2006 and 2021. We identified patients who initiated P2Y12 inhibitors ≥ 84 consecutive Defined Daily Doses (cDDDs). We estimated the risk of incident CRC and CRC mortality according to P2Y12 inhibitor use using Cox proportional-hazards regression models adjusting for potential confounders including comorbidities and regular aspirin use. We documented 4,015 incident CRC cases and 2,610 CRC-related deaths during a median follow-up of 5.1 years (IRQ, 2.1-9.0 years). We did not observe an association between P2Y12 inhibitor use and CRC incidence. In contrast, a longer duration of P2Y12 inhibitor use was associated with lower CRC-related mortality. Compared to non-users, multivariable-adjusted hazard ratio (HR) for CRC mortality were 0.73 (95% CI, 0.60-0.89) in patients with 336-671 cDDDs of P2Y12 inhibitor and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.68-0.97) in those with ≥672 cDDDs. Among patients with incident CRC diagnosis, subsequent initiation of P2Y12 inhibitor after CRC diagnosis was associated with significantly lower CRC mortality (HR 0.42; 95% CI, 0.29-0.60). P2Y12 inhibitor use was not associated with risk of incident CRC but was significantly inversely associated with CRC mortality, which appeared to be due to improved survival among individuals who initiate P2Y12 inhibitors after CRC diagnosis. These findings merit further study given the observational nature of the analysis and potential for residual confounding.

title: Peak Alpha Frequency in Context: Biomarker or Brain State?
The Receptor for Advanced Glycation End Products: Regulation and Implications in Metabolic Diseases.
abstract: Receptor for advanced glycation end-products (RAGE) was originally identified as a receptor for advanced glycation end-products; however, it can also bind a broader range of damage-associated molecular patterns, including S100 proteins, high mobility group box 1, and amyloid-β. Ligand-induced RAGE activation promotes receptor oligomerization and recruitment of diaphanous-related formin-1, which activates several intracellular cascades, leading to the production of inflammatory mediators and reactive oxygen species. RAGE expression is upregulated in disease-associated tissues, including adipose tissue in diabetes and microglia and neurons in Alzheimer's disease, and the mechanisms by which RAGE activation contributes to pathogenesis are disease-specific. The review summarizes the expression and activation of RAGE, and the potential mechanisms through which RAGE contributes to disease pathogenesis. We further discuss current and emerging strategies for modulating RAGE signaling and highlight their therapeutic potential in the prevention and treatment of RAGE-associated diseases.
keywords: Receptor for Advanced Glycation End Products

title: Towards a Better Definition of Patient-Centered Therapeutic Strategy of Parkinson's Disease: An Opinion Paper.
abstract: Recent Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment guidelines remain predominantly drug- and stage-centric and only inconsistently articulate a patient-centered medication strategy. We aimed to identify this gap and propose pragmatic, consensus-based principles for fully individualized, preference-sensitive pharmacological care across the patient journey. Seventeen movement disorder experts from eight European countries convened (March 2026) and generated key clinical questions spanning early to advanced PD. Panelists completed an anonymized questionnaire; semantic AI supported identification of areas of consensus and dissensus, followed by a single-round Delphi-style discussion to refine agreed statements. The panel reached consensus on eight statements across five focus areas: (i) incorporating patient characteristics and contextual factors underrepresented in guidelines (comorbidities, co-medications, behavioral/cognitive risk, non-motor symptom burden, and-when appropriate-genetics); (ii) treating therapy initiation as a longitudinal process with shared decision-making, education, and non-pharmacological foundations; (iii) legitimizing watchful waiting or dose reduction in selected scenarios; (iv) using both motor and non-motor symptoms and lifestyle goals as primary drivers of oral therapy selection; and (v) transparently managing evidence gaps while providing good-practice guidance on reassessment. Examples on how these recommendations can be used to plan a therapy strategy are presented for different patients' personae. In conclusion, a patient-centered medication strategy in PD should be explicit, structured, and revisited over time, aligning therapeutic choices with symptoms, risks, context, and individual goals and preferences. A wide range of treatments must always be available throughout the patient's care pathway to allow for greater individualization of care, particularly regarding treatment sequencing, drug combinations, and dosage thresholds. This requires new forms of validation beyond traditional standardized clinical trials.

title: RAPID perfusion CT in acute ischemic stroke: an educational pictorial review of common patterns, pearls, and pitfalls.
abstract: Rapid processing of Perfusion and Diffusion (RAPID) software for CT perfusion (CTP) is a valuable tool for the evaluation of acute ischemic stroke and therapeutic decision-making in extended therapeutic windows. However, automated maps should not be interpreted in isolation. A structured, pattern-based approach, integrating qualitative visual assessment with automated quantitative output and clinical information to refine therapeutic selection, remains essential to mitigate pitfalls and optimize patient care. The aim of this article is to provide an educational pictorial review based on selected illustrative cases of the most common imaging patterns, interpretive pitfalls, and technical features of CTP processed with RAPID software in acute ischemic stroke, that may serve as a practical guide for radiologists and neuroradiologists. KEY POINTS: Question How can radiologists effectively interpret automated RAPID CT perfusion maps in acute ischemic stroke while avoiding common technical traps, diagnostic pitfalls, and anatomical limitations? Findings Integrating qualitative visual assessment, quantitative RAPID outputs, and clinical-vascular data within a structured workflow minimizes diagnostic errors and optimizes patient selection for reperfusion. Critical relevance statement This educational pictorial review provides a practical, pattern-based approach to RAPID CT perfusion interpretation, highlighting clinical applications, technical limitations, software variability, and diagnostic pitfalls to advance everyday neuroradiological practice and personalized stroke management.

title: Circadian melatonin suppression and vitamin D deficiency disrupt aortic reactivity via MT1/MT2 and VDR-dependent mechanisms in rats.
journal: Pflugers Archiv : European journal of physiology
abstract: Circadian disruption and vitamin D deficiency (VDD) are increasingly prevalent and independently associated with cardiovascular dysfunction. However, their combined impact on vascular reactivity and receptor signaling remains insufficiently defined. This study investigated the independent and interactive effects of melatonin (MEL) suppression induced by continuous light (CL) or pinealectomy (Px) and VDD on vascular contractility, endothelial function, and MT1/vitamin D receptor (VDR) gene expression in rat thoracic aorta. Isolated aortic rings were subjected to cumulative concentration response curves for phenylephrine (PE) and acetylcholine (ACh). Pharmacodynamic parameters, potency (pD₂), maximal efficacy (Emax), and area under the curve (AUC) were calculated. MEL and calcitriol modulation with receptor antagonism was performed to determine receptor dependence. Relative MT1 and VDR mRNA expression was quantified using quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). CL, Px, and VDD significantly enhanced PE-induced maximal contraction, with the combined deficiency groups exhibiting the greatest augmentation of α₁-adrenergic responsiveness. In contrast, ACh-induced relaxation was selectively impaired under dual-deficiency conditions, characterized by reduced Emax without major changes in pD2, indicating compromised endothelial efficacy rather than altered receptor sensitivity. MEL attenuated vasoconstriction and enhanced relaxation in a receptor-dependent manner, whereas calcitriol potentiated contractility through VDR signaling. Notably, combined CL + VDD produced marked upregulation of MT1 (~ 10-fold) and VDR (~ 108-fold), suggesting compensatory transcriptional remodeling. Circadian disruption and VDD synergistically promote vascular hyperreactivity and endothelial dysfunction. Their convergence amplifies α₁-adrenergic signaling while impairing nitric oxide (NO) mediated relaxation, identifying a mechanistic axis linking modern light exposure and hypovitaminosis D to heightened cardiovascular risk.

title: Biomechanical Characterization of Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Cardiomyocytes by Use of Atomic Force Microscopy.
abstract: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) is not only a high-resolution imaging technique but also a sensitive tool able to study biomechanical properties of biosamples (biomolecules, cells) in native conditions-i.e., in buffered solutions (culturing media) and stable temperature (mostly 37°C). Micromechanical transducers (cantilevers) are often used to map surface stiffness geometry, elastic, and contact parameters of living cells; however, they can also be used to monitor time course of dynamic forces (beating), their rate, and other biomechanical properties of cardiomyocyte contractility. Here we describe the construction of an AFM-based biosensor setup designed to study the biomechanical properties of cardiomyocyte clusters, using standard uncoated silicon nitride cantilevers. Force-time curves (mechanocardiograms, MCG) are recorded natively and in the presence of cardiomyocyte-contraction-affecting drugs (e.g., isoproterenol, metoprolol) in the medium, under physiological conditions. The average value of contraction force and the beat rate as basic biomechanical parameters represent pharmacological indicators of different phenotype features. Robustness, low computational requirements, and optimal spatial sensitivity (detection limit 200 pN or 20 nm) are the main advantages of the presented method.

title: The role of transcranial direct current stimulaton on ataxia: a scoping review.
abstract: Cerebellar ataxias are a diverse group of hereditary and acquired disorders that impair balance, gait, posture and ocular movements. With limited treatment options, particularly in hereditary forms, neuromodulation has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach particularly the transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS). This scoping review aims to discuss the role of tDCS as a potential therapy in reducing ataxia symptoms in both hereditary and acquired forms. A total of 787 studies were found after searching Pubmed, EMBASE, and Cochrane. After removing 273 duplicates, 514 studies remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 387 studies were excluded, leaving 127 studies for full-text assessment. Following retrieval of full text, 26 was assessed for eligibility. This review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. A comprehensive literature search was performed using PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane databases. Two independent reviewers screened studies through title/abstract and full-text review, with disagreements resolved by discussion or adjudication by two additional reviewers when necessary. We included 18 studies for the final analysis. Most studies reviewed showed that tDCS is a potential option for the treatment of ataxia, however, differences among participants, neuromodulation techniques, or trial protocols may have led to differences in the clinical outcomes. Our review highlights that the vast majority of the randomized controlled studies of tDCS in neurodegenerative ataxias have demonstrated clinical beneficial effect. There are preliminary observations that tDCS in combination therapy with rehabilitation or exercise may provide greater or more functional improvements. Future multicenter studies with long term follow up of individual disease groups, supported by clinical, imaging and biological marker measurements will help address the current limitations.

Exploring sexuality, sexual well-being and intimacy in schizophrenia spectrum disorders: systematic review and meta-synthesis of qualitative studies.
journal: European archives of psychiatry and clinical neuroscience
abstract: Sexuality and intimacy are central dimensions of identity, emotional well-being, social connectedness, and quality of life. In individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs), these domains may be profoundly affected by illness-related, psychological, interpersonal, social, institutional, and treatment-related factors. Although antipsychotic-induced sexual dysfunction is clinically relevant, a broader understanding of patients' subjective experiences is needed to capture the meaning of sexuality, intimacy, and relational well-being in this population. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the ENTREQ framework. PubMed, Scopus, and PsycINFO were searched to identify qualitative and mixed-methods studies exploring patients' subjective experiences of sexuality, sexual well-being, intimate relationships, and antipsychotic-induced sexual dysfunction in SSDs. Fifteen reports from 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Thematic synthesis identified six overarching descriptive themes: (1) illness-related challenges to sexual well-being, (2) abuse and traumatic experiences, (3) beliefs about sexuality, (4) the role of the healthcare system, (5) barriers and facilitators of sexual well-being, and (6) antipsychotic-induced sexual side effects. Patients' accounts showed that sexuality was not limited to sexual functioning, but was closely connected to self-image, stigma, emotional closeness, relational opportunities, trauma, institutional restrictions, and communication with clinicians. The analytical synthesis indicated that these factors interacted through their effects on self-image, relational confidence, opportunities for intimacy, and sexual agency, potentially reinforcing vulnerability or supporting well-being and personal recovery. Sexual well-being in individuals with SSDs is shaped by medication-related, relational, psychological, and healthcare-related factors. These findings support the integration of sexuality into patient-centred psychiatric care.

title: Human-artificial intelligence collaboration for comanaging epilepsy in real time.
abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions.

title: Revisiting the muscle spindle in ALS: Implications for spinal motor network dysfunction.
journal: Pflugers Archiv : European journal of physiology
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is typically characterized by progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons. However, the contribution of afferent sensory pathways to spinal motor network disorganization has received little attention. Converging human histological evidence from multiple independent laboratories demonstrates that fusimotor (gamma) motor neuron innervation of muscle spindles degenerates in ALS while sensory endings remain morphologically intact at the end organ, although the afferent neurons and ascending sensory pathways are also affected. This dissociation creates unmodulated proprioceptive input. Spindle-derived sensory signals reach spinal interneuron circuits without fusimotor gain-control adjustment, degrading spindles from forward sensory models encoding predicted kinematic states into crude stretch receptors. We propose that this gain-control failure, compounded by the loss of associated alpha-gamma coactivation and beta skeletofusimotor denervation, constitutes an upstream driver of the spinal inhibitory interneuron circuit dysfunction documented by recent electrophysiological studies in ALS. The resulting early disinhibition, followed by maladaptive excitation, mirrors cortical ALS pathophysiology. However, transgenic mouse ALS models show selective sparing of gamma motor neurons, unlike the human disease, constituting a critical translational limitation. We present a temporal model of human ALS, linking fusimotor denervation to progressive disruption of spinal inhibitory and excitatory circuits.

title: Natural and engineered safe reinforcement learning.
abstract: Survival depends not only on maximising rewards but on minimising harm. While Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides a normative framework for adaptive decision-making, standard algorithms often fail to account for the catastrophic costs of errors during learning, in the same way as animals do. In this review, we synthesise recent advances connecting the engineering of safe RL with behavioural and systems neuroscience. We adopt a principled taxonomy distinguishing between two strategies: (1) modifying the optimisation criterion to embed safety into the learning objective, and (2) modifying the exploration process to prevent dangerous actions. We show that engineering solutions, such as worst-case optimisation, risk-sensitive objectives (e.g., conditional value at risk, CVaR), and constrained Markov decision processes (MDPs), offer precise computational accounts for anxiety, risk-aversion, and defensive reflexes. Conversely, biological mechanisms, including innate priors, interoception, and meta-control based on uncertainty, reliability and competing needs, offer robust solutions to the problem of safe exploration in artificial agents. By bridging these domains, we highlight a converging computational landscape where safety is achieved through a dynamic interplay between reactive instincts and deliberative planning.

title: Author Correction: Parkinson's disease as a somato-cognitive action network disorder.
Translational modelling of human microglia from cultures to chimeras.
abstract: Microglia play a crucial role in maintaining homeostasis of the central nervous system, whereas their dysfunction is implicated in the pathogenesis of various neurological diseases. Nevertheless, interspecific genetic differences pose challenges to translating findings from conventional rodent models. Human pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia offer a genetically relevant alternative, but these cells undergo profound transcriptomic changes and lose key homeostatic features when isolated from physiological brain cues. Accordingly, research has increasingly focused on advanced modelling platforms designed to restore the microenvironment required for in vivo microglial identity and functionality. This review examines the evolution of human microglial platforms, encompassing foundational generation protocols and multicellular integration. The discussion extends from two-dimensional co-cultures to three-dimensional brain organoids and includes human microglia chimeric models established via xenotransplantation to provide a physiological niche. In summary, the human pluripotent stem cell-based approach represents a valuable experimental pipeline for microglia research, facilitating the investigation of polygenic structures underlying human neurological diseases, from high-throughput screening to in vivo preclinical validation.
